title: Albert the Great (15 November)
hookLine: teacher of Aquinas and a scientist of plants and stars, patron of scientists

lines: A LEAF HELD TO THE LIGHT.
cards: A leaf, held up to the light. The veins branch like rivers. The edge is toothed or smooth.
One side is darker than the other. A medieval friar spent hours looking at things like this, and at birds, stones, insects and the night sky, and then he wrote it all down.
He also taught theology, ran a house of studies, served as a bishop, and had among his students a large, quiet young man named Thomas Aquinas.
The Church calls him a Doctor of the Church, and the patron of people who study the natural world.

teach.b: Albert was a German Dominican friar, a preacher and teacher, and people came to call him the Great.
He read everything he could find, including the old Greek philosopher Aristotle, whom some Christians of his day found suspect. Albert didn't.
He thought the whole world was God's work, so honest study of it could only lead toward God, never away. And he did more than read.
He wrote about plants, animals and minerals, and he said, in effect, that in these matters you have to check for yourself, by looking and testing, not just repeat what the books say.
Some of his notes are his own observations. Then the student.

Tradition tells that Thomas Aquinas was so big and so silent that his classmates called him the dumb ox. Albert, the story goes, told them that one day this ox would bellow so loud the whole world would hear.
Thomas became one of the great teachers of the Church, and Albert had seen it coming. An old thread in the Bible runs under Albert's life.

teach.h: ASK THE BEASTS; THEY WILL TEACH.
teach.b: In the book of Job, Job tells his friends to ask the animals and the birds, and the earth itself, and they will teach.
Albert's work reads like someone taking that at its word: if the world is God's work, then a plant is a kind of page. That's why the Church names him patron of those who study the natural world.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Albert the Great on 15 November; Catholic scientists and schools of science sometimes take him as patron and mark his feast with a Mass.

o: a friar who taught Aquinas and studied nature
a German king who built great cathedrals
the pope who first welcomed Aristotle

he thought the world was God's work, so honest study led toward God.

games.q: you're Albert. your classmates mock a big, silent student as the dumb ox. what do you say?
o: say nothing; it's not your business.
say that one day this ox will bellow and the world will hear.
games.why: the story goes that Albert said exactly that, and Thomas Aquinas became one of the Church's great teachers.

practice: Find one plant, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a tree outside the window, or a picture of one, and look the way Albert looked: the shape of the leaves, how they meet the stem, the color on each side, what it seems to need.
If you like, find out its name afterward. If you pray, thank God for it plainly; if not, let it hold your full attention.

wordCard.voice: Albert. A German Dominican friar, teacher of Thomas Aquinas, a writer on plants, animals and stars, a Doctor of the Church and patron of scientists.

orig.note: Latin: Albert the Great, the name he was given.

carryVoice: Your line: patron of science. For Albert, looking closely was a way of reading God's work. Rest well.
